metadata.title: Complex Analysis: Has Primitives

extraction_notes.note: The one-sentence proof idea for the main theorem is kept as a proof sketch with an alternative proves edge; rigor semi_formal (sketch rule) was left off because the finishing step rejects rigor on proofs; the main theorem's own proof is only 'sorry'.

Marked external (standard, uncited): classical complex-analysis notions and results (primitives, line integrals, Cauchy's theorem on triangles, Cauchy-Riemann) that this Lean blueprint restates; the auxiliary triangle lemmas are kept as paper.
The abstract sentence restating the main result is recorded in also_stated_at; the two sentences 'In the proof of Theorem ...' and 'To prove Lemma ...' are prose road-map pointers with no node.

nodes.name: Has primitives
nodes.statement: Given a set $U\subset\mathbb C$, for any differentiable $f:U\to\mathbb C$, there exists a differentiable $g:U\to\mathbb C$ such that $g'=f$ on $U$.
differentia: for any differentiable $f:U\to\mathbb C$, there exists a differentiable $g:U\to\mathbb C$ such that $g'=f$ on $U$
nodes.statement_short: A set $U$ has primitives if every differentiable $f$ on $U$ is the derivative $g'$ of some differentiable $g$ on $U$.
nodes.label: hasPrimitives

nodes.name: Simply connected open sets have primitives
nodes.statement: Given an open, simply connected set $U\subset\mathbb C$, $U$ has primitives, in the sense of Definition \ref{hasPrimitives}.
assumptions: an open, simply connected set $U\subset\mathbb C$
conclusions: $U$ has primitives, in the sense of Definition \ref{hasPrimitives}
also_stated_at: This project aims to formalize a proof that holomorphic functions on simply connected open sets have primitives.
nodes.label: hasPrimitivesOfSimplyConnected

nodes.name: Proof of the main theorem (placeholder)
nodes.statement: sorry
nodes.statement_short: Placeholder ('sorry'): no argument given yet.

nodes.name: Proof idea for the main theorem
nodes.statement: The idea of the proof of the main theorem is to first prove it on a convex set, and then to extend to all simply connected sets.
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: prove the convex case first, then extend to simply connected sets.

nodes.name: Convex open sets have primitives
nodes.statement: An open convex set has primitives, in the sense of Definition \ref{hasPrimitives}.
conclusions: has primitives, in the sense of Definition \ref{hasPrimitives}
nodes.label: hasPrimitivesOfConvex

nodes.name: Proof that convex open sets have primitives
nodes.statement: Consider a convex set $U$ and a point $z_0\in U$. Given a function $f$ that is holomorphic on $U$, we construct its primitive by integrating $f$ over a line from $z_0$ to $z$: for $z\in U$, \begin{equation} g(z)=\int_{z_0\to z}\ f(z)\ dz \end{equation} where $\int_{z_0\to z}$ is defined in Definition \ref{linint}. We are then left with proving that $g$ is differentiable and that $g'=f$. To do so, we compute \begin{equation} \frac{g(z+h)-g(z)}h = \frac{\int_{z_0\to z+h} f(x)\ dx-\int_{z_0\to z} f(x)\ dx}h \end{equation} which by Lemma \ref{diffOfIntegrals}, is \begin{equation} \frac{g(z+h)-g(z)}h = \frac{\int_{z\to z+h} f(x)\ dx}h . \end{equation} We then conclude using Lemma \ref{derivOfLinint}.
nodes.statement_short: Construct $g$ as the line integral of $f$ from $z_0$; difference quotient reduces via Lemma diffOfIntegrals to a short integral, then Lemma derivOfLinint.

nodes.name: Equation (1.1)
nodes.statement: g(z)=\int_{z_0\to z}\ f(z)\ dz

nodes.name: Equation (1.2)
nodes.statement: \frac{g(z+h)-g(z)}h = \frac{\int_{z_0\to z+h} f(x)\ dx-\int_{z_0\to z} f(x)\ dx}h

nodes.name: Equation (1.3)
nodes.statement: \frac{g(z+h)-g(z)}h = \frac{\int_{z\to z+h} f(x)\ dx}h .

nodes.name: Line integral $\int_{z_1\to z_2}$
nodes.statement: Given $z_1,z_2\in\mathbb C$ and a function $f:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$, the path from $z_1$ to $z_2$ is defined as \begin{equation} \gamma(t):=z_1(1-t)+z_2 t \end{equation} and $\int_{z_1\to z_2}$ is defined as the complex integral along this path.
nodes.genus: the complex integral along this path
nodes.statement_short: The straight-line path $\gamma(t)=z_1(1-t)+z_2t$ and the integral $\int_{z_1\to z_2}$ as the complex integral along it.
nodes.label: linint

nodes.name: Straight-line path $\gamma(t)$
nodes.statement: \gamma(t):=z_1(1-t)+z_2 t

nodes.name: Difference of line integrals
nodes.statement: Given a convex open set $U$, $z_0,z_1,z_2\in U$ and a function $f$ that is holomorphic on $U$ \begin{equation} \int_{z_0\to z_1} f(x)\ dx - \int_{z_0\to z_2} f(x)\ dx = \int_{z_2\to z_1} f(x)\ dx . \end{equation}
assumptions: a function $f$ that is holomorphic on $U$
conclusions: \int_{z_0\to z_1} f(x)\ dx - \int_{z_0\to z_2} f(x)\ dx = \int_{z_2\to z_1} f(x)\ dx .
nodes.statement_short: On a convex set, the difference of the integrals from $z_0$ to $z_1$ and $z_2$ is the integral from $z_2$ to $z_1$.
nodes.label: diffOfIntegrals

nodes.name: Equation (1.5)
nodes.statement: \int_{z_0\to z_1} f(x)\ dx - \int_{z_0\to z_2} f(x)\ dx = \int_{z_2\to z_1} f(x)\ dx .

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (difference of line integrals)
nodes.statement: Consider the path $z_0\to z_1\to z_2$. Since $U$ is convex, the area enclosed by this path is a subset of $U$. Therefore, by Theorem \ref{cauchyOnTriangles}, the integral of $f$ over this path is 0. We conclude the proof by splitting the path into its components.
nodes.statement_short: The triangle $z_0\to z_1\to z_2$ lies in convex $U$, so Cauchy on triangles makes its integral vanish; split into components.

nodes.name: Derivative of the line integral
nodes.statement: Given a continuous function $f:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ and $z_0\in\mathbb C$, \begin{equation} \lim_{h\to0}\frac1h\int_{z_0\to z_0+h}f(x)\ dx=f(z_0) . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: For continuous $f$, $\frac1h\int_{z_0\to z_0+h}f\to f(z_0)$ as $h\to0$.
nodes.label: derivOfLinint

nodes.name: Equation (1.6)
nodes.statement: \lim_{h\to0}\frac1h\int_{z_0\to z_0+h}f(x)\ dx=f(z_0) .

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (derivative of the line integral)
nodes.statement: Since $f$ is continuous, \begin{equation} \int_{z_0\to z_0+h}f(x)\ dx = \int_{z_0\to z_0+h}f(z_0)+o(1)\ dx = hf(z_0)+o(h) . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Continuity gives $f=f(z_0)+o(1)$ on the short segment, so the integral is $hf(z_0)+o(h)$.

nodes.name: Equation (1.7)
nodes.statement: \int_{z_0\to z_0+h}f(x)\ dx = \int_{z_0\to z_0+h}f(z_0)+o(1)\ dx = hf(z_0)+o(h) .

nodes.name: Cauchy's theorem on triangles
nodes.statement: Given $a,b,c\in\mathbb C$, and a function $f$ that is holomorphic on the triangle formed by $a,b,c$, \begin{equation} \int_{a\to b} f(x)\ dx + \int_{b\to c} f(x)\ dx + \int_{c\to a} f(x)\ dx =0 . \end{equation}
assumptions: a function $f$ that is holomorphic on the triangle formed by $a,b,c$
conclusions: \int_{a\to b} f(x)\ dx + \int_{b\to c} f(x)\ dx + \int_{c\to a} f(x)\ dx =0 .
nodes.statement_short: The integral of a holomorphic $f$ around a triangle $a\to b\to c\to a$ vanishes.
nodes.label: cauchyOnTriangles

nodes.name: Equation (1.8)
nodes.statement: \int_{a\to b} f(x)\ dx + \int_{b\to c} f(x)\ dx + \int_{c\to a} f(x)\ dx =0 .

nodes.name: Proof of Cauchy's theorem on triangles
nodes.statement: We translate $a$ and $b$ to the real line, and use Lemma \ref{cauchyOnTriangle_base}.
nodes.statement_short: Translate so $a,b$ lie on the real line and apply the real-base triangle lemma.

nodes.name: Cauchy on triangles with real base
nodes.statement: Given $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $c\in\mathbb C$, and a function $f$ that is holomorphic on the triangle formed by $a,b,c$, \begin{equation} \int_{a\to b} f(x)\ dx + \int_{b\to c} f(x)\ dx + \int_{c\to a} f(x)\ dx =0 . \end{equation}
assumptions: a function $f$ that is holomorphic on the triangle formed by $a,b,c$
conclusions: \int_{a\to b} f(x)\ dx + \int_{b\to c} f(x)\ dx + \int_{c\to a} f(x)\ dx =0 .
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy's triangle identity when two vertices $a,b$ are real.
nodes.label: cauchyOnTriangle_base

nodes.name: Equation (1.9)
nodes.statement: \int_{a\to b} f(x)\ dx + \int_{b\to c} f(x)\ dx + \int_{c\to a} f(x)\ dx =0 .

nodes.name: Proof of Cauchy on triangles with real base
nodes.statement: Let $d:=\mathcal Re(c)$. Consider the triangles $(d,b,c)$ and $(d,a,c)$. We have \begin{equation} \int_{a\to b} f(x)\ dx + \int_{b\to c} f(x)\ dx + \int_{b\to a} f(x)\ dx = \int_{a\to d} f(x)\ dx + \int_{d\to c} f(x)\ dx + \int_{c\to a} f(x)\ dx + \int_{d\to b} f(x)\ dx + \int_{b\to c} f(x)\ dx + \int_{c\to d} f(x)\ dx \end{equation} and we compute each groups of three using Lemma \ref{cauchyOnRightTriangle}.
nodes.statement_short: Split the triangle at $d=\mathcal Re(c)$ into two right triangles and apply the right-triangle lemma to each.

nodes.name: Equation (1.10)
nodes.statement: \int_{a\to b} f(x)\ dx + \int_{b\to c} f(x)\ dx + \int_{b\to a} f(x)\ dx = \int_{a\to d} f(x)\ dx + \int_{d\to c} f(x)\ dx + \int_{c\to a} f(x)\ dx + \int_{d\to b} f(x)\ dx + \int_{b\to c} f(x)\ dx + \int_{c\to d} f(x)\ dx

nodes.name: Cauchy on right triangles
nodes.statement: Given $a,b\in\mathbb R$ and $z\in\mathbb C$, and a function $f$ that is holomorphic on the triangle formed by $z,z+a,z+ib$, \begin{equation} \int_{z\to z+a} f(x)\ dx + \int_{z+a\to z+ib} f(x)\ dx + \int_{z+ib\to z} f(x)\ dx =0 . \end{equation}
assumptions: a function $f$ that is holomorphic on the triangle formed by $z,z+a,z+ib$
conclusions: \int_{z\to z+a} f(x)\ dx + \int_{z+a\to z+ib} f(x)\ dx + \int_{z+ib\to z} f(x)\ dx =0 .
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy's triangle identity for the right triangle $z,z+a,z+ib$.
nodes.label: cauchyOnRightTriangle

nodes.name: Equation (1.11)
nodes.statement: \int_{z\to z+a} f(x)\ dx + \int_{z+a\to z+ib} f(x)\ dx + \int_{z+ib\to z} f(x)\ dx =0 .

nodes.name: Proof of Cauchy on right triangles
nodes.statement: We shift the points by $z$ and use Lemma \ref{cauchyOnRightTriangle_origin}.
nodes.statement_short: Shift by $z$ and apply the lemma for the right triangle at the origin.

nodes.name: Cauchy on right triangles at the origin
nodes.statement: Given $a,b\in\mathbb R$, and a function $f$ that is holomorphic on the triangle formed by $0,a,ib$, \begin{equation} \int_{0\to a} f(x)\ dx + \int_{a\to ib} f(x)\ dx + \int_{ib\to 0} f(x)\ dx =0 . \end{equation}
assumptions: a function $f$ that is holomorphic on the triangle formed by $0,a,ib$
conclusions: \int_{0\to a} f(x)\ dx + \int_{a\to ib} f(x)\ dx + \int_{ib\to 0} f(x)\ dx =0 .
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy's triangle identity for the right triangle with vertices $0,a,ib$.
nodes.label: cauchyOnRightTriangle_origin

nodes.name: Equation (1.12)
nodes.statement: \int_{0\to a} f(x)\ dx + \int_{a\to ib} f(x)\ dx + \int_{ib\to 0} f(x)\ dx =0 .

nodes.name: Proof of Cauchy on right triangles at the origin
nodes.statement: Let $u:=\mathcal Re(f)$ and $v:=\mathcal Im(f)$. We have \begin{equation} \int_{0\to a} f(x)\ dx + \int_{a\to ib} f(x)\ dx + \int_{ib\to 0} f(x)\ dx = \int_0^a f(x)\ dx -\int_0^b if(iy)\ dy + \int_0^b f(a+y(i-a/b))(i-a/b)\ dy . \end{equation} Furthermore, \begin{equation} \int_0^b f(a+y(i-a/b))\ dy -\int_0^b f(iy)\ dy = \int_0^b\int_0^{a-ya/b}\ \partial_x f(x+iy)dxdy \end{equation} so \begin{equation} \int_0^a f(x)\ dx -\int_0^b if(iy)\ dy + \int_0^b f(a+y(i-a/b))(i-a/b)\ dy = i\int_0^b\int_0^{a-ya/b}\ \partial_x f(x+iy)dxdx - \frac ab \int_0^b f(a+y(i-a/b))\ dy + \int_0^a f(x)\ dx . \end{equation} Now, changing variables to $x=a-ya/b$, \begin{equation} \frac ab \int_0^b f(a+y(i-a/b))\ dy = \int_0^a f(ib+x(1-ib/a))\ dx \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \int_0^a f(ib+x(1-ib/a))\ dx - \int_0^a f(x)\ dx = \int_0^a\int_0^{b-xb/a)}\partial_yf(x+iy)\ dydx . \end{equation} All in all, \begin{equation} \int_{0\to a} f(x)\ dx + \int_{a\to ib} f(x)\ dx + \int_{ib\to 0} f(x)\ dx = i\int_0^b\int_0^{a-ya/b}\ \partial_x f(x+iy)dxdy - \int_0^a\int_0^{b-xb/a)}\partial_yf(x+iy)\ dydx . \end{equation} That is, \begin{equation} \int_{0\to a} f(x)\ dx + \int_{a\to ib} f(x)\ dx + \int_{ib\to 0} f(x)\ dx = i\int_0^b\int_0^{a-ya/b}\ (\partial_x u-\partial_y v)dxdy - \int_0^a\int_0^{b-xb/a)}(\partial_yu+\partial_x v)\ dydx . \end{equation} Now by Theorem \ref{cauchyRiemann}, \begin{equation} \partial_x u=\partial_y v ,\quad \partial_y u=-\partial_x v \end{equation} so \begin{equation} \int_{0\to a} f(x)\ dx + \int_{a\to ib} f(x)\ dx + \int_{ib\to 0} f(x)\ dx = 0 . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Parametrize the three sides and rewrite the sum as double integrals of $\partial_x f$ and $\partial_y f$; Cauchy-Riemann makes it vanish.

nodes.name: Equation (1.13)
nodes.statement: \int_{0\to a} f(x)\ dx + \int_{a\to ib} f(x)\ dx + \int_{ib\to 0} f(x)\ dx = \int_0^a f(x)\ dx -\int_0^b if(iy)\ dy + \int_0^b f(a+y(i-a/b))(i-a/b)\ dy .

nodes.name: Equation (1.14)
nodes.statement: \int_0^b f(a+y(i-a/b))\ dy -\int_0^b f(iy)\ dy = \int_0^b\int_0^{a-ya/b}\ \partial_x f(x+iy)dxdy

nodes.name: Equation (1.15)
nodes.statement: \int_0^a f(x)\ dx -\int_0^b if(iy)\ dy + \int_0^b f(a+y(i-a/b))(i-a/b)\ dy = i\int_0^b\int_0^{a-ya/b}\ \partial_x f(x+iy)dxdx - \frac ab \int_0^b f(a+y(i-a/b))\ dy + \int_0^a f(x)\ dx .

nodes.name: Equation (1.16)
nodes.statement: \frac ab \int_0^b f(a+y(i-a/b))\ dy = \int_0^a f(ib+x(1-ib/a))\ dx

nodes.name: Equation (1.17)
nodes.statement: \int_0^a f(ib+x(1-ib/a))\ dx - \int_0^a f(x)\ dx = \int_0^a\int_0^{b-xb/a)}\partial_yf(x+iy)\ dydx .

nodes.name: Equation (1.18)
nodes.statement: \int_{0\to a} f(x)\ dx + \int_{a\to ib} f(x)\ dx + \int_{ib\to 0} f(x)\ dx = i\int_0^b\int_0^{a-ya/b}\ \partial_x f(x+iy)dxdy - \int_0^a\int_0^{b-xb/a)}\partial_yf(x+iy)\ dydx .

nodes.name: Equation (1.19)
nodes.statement: \int_{0\to a} f(x)\ dx + \int_{a\to ib} f(x)\ dx + \int_{ib\to 0} f(x)\ dx = i\int_0^b\int_0^{a-ya/b}\ (\partial_x u-\partial_y v)dxdy - \int_0^a\int_0^{b-xb/a)}(\partial_yu+\partial_x v)\ dydx .

nodes.name: Equation (1.20)
nodes.statement: \partial_x u=\partial_y v ,\quad \partial_y u=-\partial_x v

nodes.name: Equation (1.21)
nodes.statement: \int_{0\to a} f(x)\ dx + \int_{a\to ib} f(x)\ dx + \int_{ib\to 0} f(x)\ dx = 0 .

nodes.name: Cauchy-Riemann equations
nodes.statement: If $f:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ is differentiable at $z\in\mathbb C$, then, denoting $z=x+iy$, \begin{equation} \partial_x\mathcal Re(f(z))=\partial_y\mathcal Im(f(z)) ,\quad \partial_y\mathcal Re(f(z))=-\partial_x\mathcal Im(f(z)) \end{equation}
assumptions: $f:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ is differentiable at $z\in\mathbb C$
nodes.statement_short: A complex-differentiable $f$ satisfies the Cauchy-Riemann equations for its real and imaginary parts.
nodes.label: cauchyRiemann

nodes.name: Cauchy-Riemann equations (1.22)
nodes.statement: \partial_x\mathcal Re(f(z))=\partial_y\mathcal Im(f(z)) ,\quad \partial_y\mathcal Re(f(z))=-\partial_x\mathcal Im(f(z))

nodes.name: Proof of the Cauchy-Riemann equations
nodes.statement: Since $f$ is differentiable, for $a\in\mathbb R$, \begin{equation} \lim_{a\to0}\frac{f(z+a)-f(z)}a=\frac{f(z+ia)-f(z)}{ia} \end{equation} that is \begin{equation} \partial_x f(z)=-i\partial_y f(z) \end{equation} from which we conclude.
nodes.statement_short: Compare the difference quotient along real and imaginary directions: $\partial_x f=-i\partial_y f$.

nodes.name: Equation (1.23)
nodes.statement: \lim_{a\to0}\frac{f(z+a)-f(z)}a=\frac{f(z+ia)-f(z)}{ia}

nodes.name: Equation (1.24)
nodes.statement: \partial_x f(z)=-i\partial_y f(z)

nodes.name: Construct candidate primitive
nodes.statement: Consider a convex set $U$ and a point $z_0\in U$. Given a function $f$ that is holomorphic on $U$, we construct its primitive by integrating $f$ over a line from $z_0$ to $z$: for $z\in U$, \begin{equation} g(z)=\int_{z_0\to z}\ f(z)\ dz \end{equation} where $\int_{z_0\to z}$ is defined in Definition \ref{linint}.
nodes.statement_short: Define $g(z)$ as the line integral of $f$ from $z_0$ to $z$.

nodes.name: Reduce to differentiability
nodes.statement: We are then left with proving that $g$ is differentiable and that $g'=f$.
nodes.statement_short: It remains to show $g$ is differentiable with $g'=f$.

nodes.name: Difference quotient
nodes.statement: To do so, we compute \begin{equation} \frac{g(z+h)-g(z)}h = \frac{\int_{z_0\to z+h} f(x)\ dx-\int_{z_0\to z} f(x)\ dx}h \end{equation} which by Lemma \ref{diffOfIntegrals}, is \begin{equation} \frac{g(z+h)-g(z)}h = \frac{\int_{z\to z+h} f(x)\ dx}h . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Write the difference quotient and simplify it with Lemma diffOfIntegrals.

nodes.name: Conclude via derivative lemma
nodes.statement: We then conclude using Lemma \ref{derivOfLinint}.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude with Lemma derivOfLinint.

nodes.name: Triangle inside U
nodes.statement: Consider the path $z_0\to z_1\to z_2$. Since $U$ is convex, the area enclosed by this path is a subset of $U$.
nodes.statement_short: The triangle $z_0\to z_1\to z_2$ lies in $U$ by convexity.

nodes.name: Apply Cauchy on triangles
nodes.statement: Therefore, by Theorem \ref{cauchyOnTriangles}, the integral of $f$ over this path is 0.
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy on triangles: the integral over the closed path is 0.

nodes.name: Split the path
nodes.statement: We conclude the proof by splitting the path into its components.
nodes.statement_short: Split the closed path into its segments to get the identity.

nodes.name: Introduce d and sub-triangles
nodes.statement: Let $d:=\mathcal Re(c)$. Consider the triangles $(d,b,c)$ and $(d,a,c)$.
nodes.statement_short: Set $d=\mathcal Re(c)$ and consider triangles $(d,b,c)$, $(d,a,c)$.

nodes.name: Decompose and apply right-triangle lemma
nodes.statement: We have \begin{equation} \int_{a\to b} f(x)\ dx + \int_{b\to c} f(x)\ dx + \int_{b\to a} f(x)\ dx = \int_{a\to d} f(x)\ dx + \int_{d\to c} f(x)\ dx + \int_{c\to a} f(x)\ dx + \int_{d\to b} f(x)\ dx + \int_{b\to c} f(x)\ dx + \int_{c\to d} f(x)\ dx \end{equation} and we compute each groups of three using Lemma \ref{cauchyOnRightTriangle}.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the triangle integral as two right-triangle sums and apply Lemma cauchyOnRightTriangle.

nodes.name: Parametrize the sides
nodes.statement: Let $u:=\mathcal Re(f)$ and $v:=\mathcal Im(f)$. We have \begin{equation} \int_{0\to a} f(x)\ dx + \int_{a\to ib} f(x)\ dx + \int_{ib\to 0} f(x)\ dx = \int_0^a f(x)\ dx -\int_0^b if(iy)\ dy + \int_0^b f(a+y(i-a/b))(i-a/b)\ dy . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Set $u=\mathcal Re f$, $v=\mathcal Im f$ and parametrize the three sides.

nodes.name: Fundamental theorem in x
nodes.statement: Furthermore, \begin{equation} \int_0^b f(a+y(i-a/b))\ dy -\int_0^b f(iy)\ dy = \int_0^b\int_0^{a-ya/b}\ \partial_x f(x+iy)dxdy \end{equation} so \begin{equation} \int_0^a f(x)\ dx -\int_0^b if(iy)\ dy + \int_0^b f(a+y(i-a/b))(i-a/b)\ dy = i\int_0^b\int_0^{a-ya/b}\ \partial_x f(x+iy)dxdx - \frac ab \int_0^b f(a+y(i-a/b))\ dy + \int_0^a f(x)\ dx . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Express a difference of edge integrals as a double integral of $\partial_x f$ and rewrite the sum.

nodes.name: Change of variables
nodes.statement: Now, changing variables to $x=a-ya/b$, \begin{equation} \frac ab \int_0^b f(a+y(i-a/b))\ dy = \int_0^a f(ib+x(1-ib/a))\ dx \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \int_0^a f(ib+x(1-ib/a))\ dx - \int_0^a f(x)\ dx = \int_0^a\int_0^{b-xb/a)}\partial_yf(x+iy)\ dydx . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Change variables $x=a-ya/b$ and express another difference as a double integral of $\partial_y f$.

nodes.name: Combine
nodes.statement: All in all, \begin{equation} \int_{0\to a} f(x)\ dx + \int_{a\to ib} f(x)\ dx + \int_{ib\to 0} f(x)\ dx = i\int_0^b\int_0^{a-ya/b}\ \partial_x f(x+iy)dxdy - \int_0^a\int_0^{b-xb/a)}\partial_yf(x+iy)\ dydx . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Combine into a difference of two double integrals of partial derivatives.

nodes.name: Rewrite in u and v
nodes.statement: That is, \begin{equation} \int_{0\to a} f(x)\ dx + \int_{a\to ib} f(x)\ dx + \int_{ib\to 0} f(x)\ dx = i\int_0^b\int_0^{a-ya/b}\ (\partial_x u-\partial_y v)dxdy - \int_0^a\int_0^{b-xb/a)}(\partial_yu+\partial_x v)\ dydx . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the integrands in terms of $u$ and $v$.

nodes.name: Apply Cauchy-Riemann
nodes.statement: Now by Theorem \ref{cauchyRiemann}, \begin{equation} \partial_x u=\partial_y v ,\quad \partial_y u=-\partial_x v \end{equation} so \begin{equation} \int_{0\to a} f(x)\ dx + \int_{a\to ib} f(x)\ dx + \int_{ib\to 0} f(x)\ dx = 0 . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The Cauchy-Riemann equations make both integrands vanish.
